html:
My last night at home on this 2024 Chinese New Year break.

We had planned to take the train back to H City, but on the way here the train had been packed, and since K isn’t where the line starts, there was nowhere at all to put our three suitcases. So we decided to hire a car and driver. The driver is someone my cousin knows; she hires him often. In a small place, nothing gets things done like favors and connections. I booked him before New Year, but he kept saying to message him on WeChat the day before the trip, because if you book too far ahead he worries about being stood up. I told him our flights were already booked, so there was no way we’d cancel, and besides, there was the connection through my cousin. That set his mind at rest, and he kept the fourth day of the first lunar month free for us. Today I sent him our home address and set a time: 9:30 tomorrow morning. He said, how about eight? He has a birthday party to go to and is worried that if he leaves late he won’t make it. I said that was too early. He said, half past eight then, any later and he’s worried he won’t make it. I said we have elderly people with us, we want a bit more rest in the morning, and the flight is in the evening anyway. He said, doesn’t your hotel screenshot show you’re staying a night? You can rest there. I didn’t explain any further, just said 9:30 is the earliest. After a while he said, fine, 9:30. It feels less like I’m hiring his car and more like I’ve hired a car to take him to his party. You don’t get this kind of problem with the big ride-hailing platforms. It’s arrangements like this, running on gentlemen’s agreements plus connections, that produce this sort of nonsense. I sent the screenshots to my cousin and asked whether he’s reliable. She said he is. I have chosen to trust her connection, and I hope everything goes smoothly tomorrow.

Today I helped my parents sort out their things and pack. This used to be Dad’s job, no question, but since I got back this time, I can see him aging before my eyes. He often forgets things, his reactions are a little slower, and he is no longer as industrious as he used to be; Mom is always grumbling about it. If I hadn’t stepped in, the packing might not have started until the afternoon. I got a bit impatient waiting and just dived in myself. They thought I packed fast and well. I said, “I’ve been doing this for more than ten years, like it or not!” I can feel our roles gradually reversing: from the child my parents looked after, I have slowly become the one they lean on. A few years ago, when I first started taking them traveling, I felt a sense of accomplishment: they were happy to see me grown up, and I was happy not to be a child anymore. In the last couple of years the novelty has worn off, and I have started to feel the weight on my shoulders. Now and then I can’t help thinking further ahead. If one of them were gone, what would the other do? What would I do? Then I feel guilty, as if I shouldn’t think like that, and the two feelings keep taking turns.

Another thing I have to get used to is the constant outward display of filial devotion, mostly in words. Before I came back, my parents transferred quite a lot of euros to me; I was surprised by how much. I know that if they didn’t, they would feel bad, since we have only just started building up savings. Their generation has an almost ritual fixation when traveling: you have to buy clothes along the way. “You can’t go on a trip and not buy a single piece of clothing!” That, I have discovered, is the unspoken consensus of their generation. So when packing, my view was to bring enough clothes; theirs was to bring some and buy whatever they’re short of. The test of filial devotion, and the logic behind it, goes like this: if they say they won’t bring many clothes, my next line should be, “Just buy them when we get there!” But deep down I have an instinctive aversion to this kind of lip-service filial piety, so I didn’t say that line out loud. The result was that today, while we packed, they kept repeating themselves, and I kept responding without much enthusiasm. Perhaps, deep down, they felt a small pang of disappointment.

I need to keep working on myself: accept that they are entering old age, be patient with how their thinking and their way of talking are changing, adjust my attitude, and get ready for the three months together that lie ahead!

Here’s to a smooth journey tomorrow.
